working: The line opens with an alto clef and a three-sharp key signature (A major). The first stretch, before the first barline, is five beamed notes on one pitch: a short note, three longer ones and a short one. That is the end of bar 70: e'16 e'8 e'8 e'8 e'16. So the line picks up bar 70 partway through, after the dis' notes that ended the previous line. After the barline come eight groups of four 32nds. The first group is lower (e'), the next two are higher (a'), and the fourth drops (fis'). The last four groups sit higher still (b'). The edition writes those b' groups as b'4:32 b'4:32, and the copyist writes them out in full. Together this is bar 71. After the second barline come four groups of four 32nds, all on e'. That is the first half of bar 72 (e'32 ×16). The line ends with a custos (the wavy mark pointing to the next note), so the rest of bar 72 (e'4:32 e'4:32) carries over to the next line. Nothing contradicts the edition.
insights: The barlines are clear, and the pitch contour of bar 71 (low, high, high, lower, then highest) fixes the match. The repeated notes on one pitch at the start and end needed counting rhythm and groups to place them within bars 70 and 72. Clearer stems and beams on the opening syncopated figure would have made its rhythm easier to confirm. Knowing that the edition's tremolo marks stand for written-out 32nds also helps.

working: The line opens with the alto clef and the A-major key signature. Next come five beamed notes, all on e'. They match the second half of bar 70, which is e'16 e'8 e'8 e'8 e'16. The first half of bar 70 (the dis'/e' figure) must be on the line before, so the line starts partway through bar 70. After the first barline there are groups of 32nd notes: one group of four low notes (e'), two groups higher (a'), and one group lower again (fis'). Then come four high groups beamed together (b'), the copyist's way of writing the b'4:32 b'4:32 tremolo. That is bar 71. After the second barline there are four more 32nd-note groups at about the same height. That fits e' repeated 16 times, the first half of bar 72. A '~' then stands for the rest of the bar, the e'4:32 e'4:32 tremolo. This can't be bar 73: it would drop from e' to a and fis below it and end in 16ths (b2:16). So the line ends in bar 72, and it holds bars 70 to 72, not 70 to 71.
insights: Bars 70 and 71 were easy to find: the five e' notes match bar 70's second half, and bar 71 has a clear rise and fall (e', a', fis', b'). The third bar is harder because the copyist cut it short with a '~' repeat sign, and bars 72 and 73 both open with 32nd-note groups. Clear note heights in the third bar would make it easier to tell bar 72 from bar 73. So would treating repeat signs like '~' as standing for the rest of a bar.

insights: This line was hard to match because nearly every note is the same repeated 32nd, on a or a'. The only real landmarks are the jump from a to a' in bar 86 and the two barlines. The partial bars at each end can only be placed by counting beam groups, and the small, crowded beams make that uncertain. Dynamics in the edition text, here the cresc. and f, would have confirmed the bar placement directly.
